Unit price tells us which box is the better deal, but it is not the only thing a family should think about.

tasks.title: Two Letters From the Archive
tasks.scenario: A history club is preparing an exhibit about the night electric streetlights were switched on in Marlow, a fictional town, in 1912. Two made-up letters from the archive describe that night. A visitor asks how the two writers see the event.
tasks.prompt: Listen to the two fictional letters. Compare the writers' perspectives: what each person thinks about the streetlights and the reason each gives. Then explain one reason their views may be different.

turns.speaker: Ruth Calloway, shopkeeper (fictional)
turns.text: Dear Aunt, last night the town switched on thirty electric streetlights along Main Street. The whole street glowed. I kept my bakery open two hours longer, and I sold more bread than on any other evening this month. I believe the streetlights will bring more customers to every shop in Marlow.

turns.speaker: Elias Hart, lamplighter (fictional)
turns.text: To the town council: for eleven years I have walked Main Street every evening to light the gas lamps. Last night, thirty electric lights replaced the gas lamps I tended. I am glad the street is bright, but I do not know what work I will have next month. The council has not said whether lamplighters will be kept on.

listenFor: what each writer thinks about the streetlights
the reason each writer gives
what each writer is worried or happy about

check.q: Why does Ruth believe the streetlights are good for Marlow?

The lights are cheaper than gas.
The lights keep thieves away.

check.q: How does Elias feel about the streetlights?

Sure that the streetlights are a mistake.
Happy because he will get a new job.
check.why: He is glad the street is bright, but he does not know what work he will have because the council has not said whether lamplighters stay.

guided.model: Ruth, the shopkeeper, thinks the streetlights are good news because she kept her bakery open longer and sold more bread. She believes they will bring more customers to every shop. Elias, the lamplighter, is glad the street is bright, but he is worried because electric lights replaced the gas lamps he tended and the council has not said whether he will keep his work. Both writers noticed that the street is brighter, but Ruth looks at what she gains while Elias looks at what he might lose. Their perspectives may be different because their jobs are affected in different ways. These are fictional letters, so we would need more sources to know how the whole town felt.
